features.headline: Three Jaguars trade deadline takeaways, from 'F them picks' to BTJ staying
features.desc: The 6-2 Jaguars aggressively upgraded their defense at the deadline and kept the offense intact. Let's look at the aftermath of the three deals.
body: JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — Jacksonville Jaguars general manager James Gladstone doesn't want to call the three trades he made Monday to fortify the secondary and defensive line "going all-in" to get to the Super Bowl.

"I characterize it as getting better as a football team and prioritizing getting better as a football team," he said. "I look forward to seeing it all come to life and being a part of bringing it to life here this week and beyond."
He might not like it, but going all-in is probably the most accurate way to describe what the Jaguars did on the day before the NFL's trade deadline.

They sent a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles for defensive tackle Jordan Davis, sent a 2027-second round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Atlanta Falcons for safety Jessie Bates III and sent a conditional 2027 sixth-round pick to the New Orleans Saints for defensive tackle Davon Godchaux.

That's five draft picks, including three premium selections, for three veteran players. All three players plug holes in the roster created by season-ending injuries to nose tackle DaVon Hamilton (quad) and safety Eric Murray (elbow).
And as a bonus, two of the three have appeared in Super Bowls: Davis has played in two and won one with the Eagles, and Bates has played in one with the Cincinnati Bengals.
"Huge for us to be able to continue to add to our already talented roster and competitive group," head coach Liam Coen said.

Those three trades were finalized over a nine-hour period on Monday, starting with Bates just before 8 a.m. ET, continuing with Godchaux around 1 p.m. ET and concluding with Davis shortly before 5 p.m. ET.

features.headline: How Cubs' Pete-Crow Armstrong became runaway NL MVP favorite
features.desc: The Cubs' star center fielder hit another level midway through the 2026 season. Here's what shaped PCA's superstar turn.
body: It's easy to forget that Pete Crow-Armstrong was having a quiet first six weeks of the 2026 MLB season after signing a six-year, $115 million contract extension a few months earlier.

The moment that turned the Chicago Cubs center fielder into a runaway favorite for National League MVP honors didn't come until mid-May — in a matchup against the Atlanta Braves and 2024 Cy Young winner Chris Sale.

Crow-Armstrong's defense, as usual, had been outstanding. But while batting ninth in the order during the early portion of the year, he had yet to find his groove at the plate and was batting just.238 with a.679 OPS.
Cubs hitting coach John Mallee attempted a "we have nothing to lose moment" against the nasty left-hander. The Cubs decided to move the lefty-hitting Crow-Armstrong closer to the plate.
"You're either going to get hit or the ball's going forward," Mallee recalled saying to Crow-Armstrong going into the game. "There's only two options because you're standing on top of the plate now."
It was similar to what former Cubs star Anthony Rizzo tried years earlier under Mallee's tutelage.

Back then, when Mallee expressed concern for Rizzo's health — as his hit by pitch totals increased — the former All-Star first baseman famously reminded Mallee that he had survived cancer so he wasn't much afraid of a baseball.
Crow-Armstrong decided he was up for the challenge after talking to Rizzo about it. He wanted to get on base more. Getting hit was one way.

Crow-Armstrong didn't get hit, but he did go 1-for-2 off Sale that day. He turned on a 97 mph pitch for a single in the second then grounded out on a 3-1 count in the fifth. They were not headline generating plays, but they were the genesis for the months filled with such moments ahead.

features.headline: Who will win MVP? Picks, analysis for 2026 MLB awards week
features.desc: Baseball's best players and managers of 2026 collect their hardware this week.
body: The baseball offseason has felt pretty normal so far if you can put the overhanging labor negotiations out of your mind.
Some of that normalcy comes from the gradual easing into the initial phases of the hot stove season — contract options, roster maneuvering, free agency filing — that point toward next season.
That's administrative stuff, though, and not as fun as the parade in Milwaukee — or this week, when MLB is handing out its major awards in what closes the books on the 2026 season.
This year's awards week added a new honor being handed out by the Baseball Writers' Association of America: the Reliever of the Year Award, which recognizes the top bullpen maestro from each league.
Here's how the rest of this week's schedule lays out:
Below, we break down the major award winners so far — and preview Thursday's grand finale.
MVP | Cy Young | Reliever of the Year Rookie of the Year | Manager of the Year
Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals
What to know: Here are the OPS+ figures for the qualifying hitters who ranked second through sixth in the AL: 153, 149, 148, 146 and 144. No. 1? That would be Alvarez... at 190.
He dominated the leaderboards for AL hitters at a Wilt Chamberlain-like level, sweeping all the slash categories and falling one homer and seven RBIs shy of a Triple Crown.

Alvarez made that production count, pacing AL hitters in win probability added (6.9), with a figure that was 68% better than the second-place finisher, Pete Alonso. At 81-81, Alvarez's Astros barely eked out a postseason spot. Without him, they would have been lottery-bound for sure.

features.headline: Why 2-7 Jets preferred to keep roster intact at trade deadline
features.desc: A year after making two blockbuster trades, New York stayed quiet at the NFL trade deadline.
body: FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — One year after rocking the NFL with the Sauce Gardner and Quinnen Williams blockbusters at the trade deadline, the New York Jets made no splashy deals despite obvious roster needs and a handful of players that would've fetched nice returns.

Ahead of Tuesday's deadline, general manager Darren Mougey was quiet — well, except for a minor trade involving backup safety Andre Cisco, who was sent to the Detroit Lions for a 2029 sixth-round pick.
The Jets were only interested in trading players on expiring contracts (like Cisco), preferring to keep their 2027 roster intact.
While some might argue that a team with 21 losses in its last 26 games should've reached for the sun and moon to improve its future, the Jets sent three messages by standing (almost) pat:

Plus, let's be honest, there also was a subliminal message: With Glenn on the hot seat, they wanted to wait until the coaching dust settles in the offseason before selling off players that might intrigue a new coaching staff.
Explaining their approach to the deadline, Glenn said Wednesday, "[Our] philosophy hasn't changed from last year."
He said they will always listen to inquiries, but "we won't force any issues, and we'll make sure we do what's best for the organization."
Glenn likes the current roster, claiming, "We're right on the cusp of trying to break through."

He noted that the Jets have lost five one-score games against a tough schedule. In fact, they're 1-5 in one-score games, 4-10 in two seasons under Glenn. Based on their opponents' records, the Jets' strength of schedule ranks 23rd, per ESPN Analytics.

features.headline: From Ballon d'Or hopes to Real Madrid bench: Should Liverpool re-sign Trent Alexander-Arnold?
features.desc: Trent Alexander-Arnold's dream move to Real Madrid is turning into a nightmare, but would Liverpool take him back? And would he want to return?
body: It was two years ago that Trent Alexander-Arnold sat down at Liverpool's AXA Training Centre and made the admission that would signal the beginning of the end of his Anfield career.

During an interview with Sky Sports, the defender was asked which dream he would most like to realize: would he rather captain Liverpool, win another Champions League title, win a trophy with England, or win the Ballon d'Or? Surprisingly, he settled on the latter option.
"I believe I can," Alexander-Arnold said. "I want to be the first full back to ever do it."
In a world where footballers — whether sincerely or not — are often quick to downplay the importance of individual accolades versus team success, it was a bold choice.

Six months later, Alexander-Arnold announced he would be leaving his boyhood club to join Real Madrid, who paid Liverpool €12 million so the right back would be available to feature at the FIFA Club World Cup ahead of his contract expiring that summer.

Madrid's desire to expedite the start of Alexander-Arnold's journey at the club was a reflection of how keen the Spanish giants were on his signing. Nearly 18 months on, though, and his career has stalled.

Across his time in Madrid so far, the 28-year-old has started just 18 out of a possible 50 LaLiga games. Injuries have played a part, as has the significant managerial churn at the Bernabeu, but it increasingly feels like the defender's dream move is turning into a nightmare.
Jose Mourinho's appointment as head coach in July has further complicated matters.

features.headline: Who has scored the most goals in NHL history?
features.desc: Alex Ovechkin holds the record for the most individual career goals in NHL history. Which other players are at the top of the list?
body: At the time of his retirement in 1999, Wayne Gretzky owned or shared 61 NHL records, including the mark for the most career goals. "The Great One" finished his illustrious 20-year career with an NHL-record 894 goals in 1,487 games. It is a mark that stood until Alex Ovechkin broke it in April 2025.

With Gretzky in attendance, Ovechkin scored his 895th career goal in a 4-1 loss to the New York Islanders. Ovechkin's record-breaking goal came in the 1,487th game of his NHL career, the same as Gretzky's career total.
The 2026-27 NHL season marks the 22nd for Ovechkin, who looks to add to his career goals total and put even more separation between him and the rest of the field.
